definition: Vitriolic means filled with bitter, cruel harshness.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vitriolic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vitriolic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The two Victorian orchid hunters filled a decade with vitriolic letters, each accusing the other of theft, fraud, and 'a greenhouse run on lies.'
A sharp remark has an edge but no venom — the mild end of the ladder, far below vitriolic.
Cutting words wound and are meant to, yet they stop short of vitriolic, where the wound is doused in acid — bitterness added for the pleasure of the burn.

Poisonous words are meant to injure, like venom worked into words — the harm is the whole intention. Vitriolic overlaps closely but names the chemistry: bitterness like acid, cruel and burning on contact. Poison suggests quiet, hidden damage; vitriol scars in the open, the moment it lands.

A savage attack comes at full, unrestrained force — nothing held back, no line uncrossed. Vitriolic adds bitterness to the force: acid, spite, cruelty savored. A savage review may simply be merciless about the work; a vitriolic one wants the author to feel the burn.

Vitriolic means filled with bitter, cruel harshness.
The town-hall meeting about parking turned vitriolic within minutes — a retired teacher was called a saboteur over a crosswalk, and two neighbors of forty years left by different doors.
Vitriolic is more precise than 'angry' or 'harsh' because it names language with acid in it — bitter, cruel, and meant to burn what it lands on.
An angry letter wants to win the argument; a vitriolic one wants to leave a scar.
Vitriolic is for language past saving — feuds, flame wars, poison-pen letters.
Its unit-mate acerbic is the crucial calibration: acerbic stings with wit and can even improve its target, while vitriolic has burned the wit off and means only to hurt.
If you can laugh, it was acerbic; if you flinch, it was vitriolic.

In the 1920s, Chicago theatergoers bought two papers on opening nights: one for Enid Marsh's review, one for Carl Baum's reply to it.
What began as professional disagreement turned vitriolic within a season.
Marsh called Baum's prose 'a fog with opinions.' Baum answered that Marsh praised only plays short enough to finish before her deadline.
Editors at both papers loved the feud and kept score; the playwrights caught between them did not.
One director recalled a notice so acid that he checked the byline twice — the play was barely mentioned, the rival critic burned in every line.
